text: Giordano worked so fast that people nicknamed him Luca fa presto, which means Luca paints quickly. He trained with Ribera around 1650. His father Antonio was a painter, and Ribera's half length philosophers shaped Giordano, who painted many of them himself. Around 1652 he went to Rome for the first time and studied the Baroque art of Pietro da Cortona. He also earned the names The Thunderbolt and The Proteus of painting, since he could imitate other painters so well. Later he worked in Naples, Rome, Florence and Venice before ten years in Spain.

Italians nicknamed Honthorst Gherardo delle Notti, or Gerard of the Nights, for his scenes lit by artificial light. He was born in Utrecht, trained with his father, a decorative painter, and then with Abraham Bloemaert. In Rome he lodged at the palace of Vincenzo Giustiniani, where he painted Christ Before the High Priest. Cardinal Scipione Borghese became another patron. He came back to Utrecht in 1620. Queen Elizabeth of Bohemia, living in exile in the Netherlands, employed him as a painter and as a drawing master for her children, and through her Charles I invited him to England in 1628.

The Royal Danish Academy in Copenhagen turned Tidemand away at first. He studied at a private art school and soon became a pupil at the academy anyway. From 1837 he studied in Düsseldorf under Theodor Hildebrandt. In Hardanger he met the 18 year old Hans Gude, and the two became close friends who made landscape paintings together, with Tidemand adding the figures. He travelled around Norway to study folk costumes, tools and buildings. In 1848 King Oscar I asked him to paint a series of Norwegian peasant life for the palace of Oscarshall.

Macke lived most of his creative life in Bonn, with short stays at Lake Thun and trips to Paris, Italy, the Netherlands and Tunisia. His father was a building contractor and amateur artist, and his drawings were the first art to impress the boy. Macke enrolled at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf in 1904, the year his father died. In Paris in 1907 he saw the Impressionists, and soon afterwards he spent a few months in Lovis Corinth's studio in Berlin. Through his friend Franz Marc he met Kandinsky. He died in the First World War.

Hackert's pictures of the Battle of Chesma were made for Catherine the Great, and some of his battle scenes hang in the Peterhof palace in Russia. He grew up in Prenzlau in Brandenburg, trained with his father, a portraitist and animal painter, and went to the Prussian Academy in Berlin. In Paris he worked mostly in gouache. He left for Italy in 1768 and settled mainly in Rome and Naples, where he produced many works for Sir William Hamilton. Goethe became his friend when he visited Naples in 1786. Goethe also wrote the first biography of Hackert.

Isabey drew himself and his family in a picture called Boat, and it was a success at the Salon of 1820. At 19 he became a pupil of Jacques-Louis David after lessons from the miniature painter François Dumont. He painted the dukes of Angoulême and Berry for the Palace of Versailles. Josephine and Napoleon Bonaparte both backed him, and he planned the ceremonies for their coronation and prepared drawings for the book that recorded it. Several rulers gave him commissions until his death in 1855. His son Eugène painted seascapes.

König made more than 100 transparent paintings, and he showed them by candlelight to paying audiences. He started in his father's trade as a decorative painter in Bern, then studied with Marquard Wocher and Sigmund Freudenberger and learned printmaking from Balthasar Anton Dunker. In 1797 the family left Bern for the Bernese Oberland, where he made coloured etchings, lithographs and small oil paintings for visitors. His costume pictures and scenes of country life came out as popular print series. In 1811 he began showing his Diaphanorama in Bern. Later he toured with it.

De Zwart's father painted carriages, and at 14 the boy was apprenticed to a carriage maker to learn the same trade. In his spare time he copied prints from magazines, and a year later he joined the evening class at the Royal Academy in The Hague. Maris took him into his studio. Jacob Maris once sent him to the coast without drawing materials and made him paint his impressions straight onto canvas when he got back. At the Mauritshuis he copied Vermeer, Potter and Rembrandt. People call him the Hague Breitner for his likeness to George Hendrik Breitner.

Hodges first made a living by painting theatre scenery, after he studied under William Shipley and in the studio of Richard Wilson. Between 1772 and 1775 he sailed with James Cook as the expedition's artist. The big oil paintings from that trip were finished in London, where the Admiralty paid him a salary to complete them. Critics complained that his strong light and colour contrasts made the pictures look rough and unfinished. In 1780 he went to India under the patronage of Warren Hastings. His Benares sketches later became the base for The Ghauts at Benares.

Houbraken says Visscher was an able etcher who had an unusual talent for drawing live models in charcoal. He was born and died in Haarlem, and he trained with Pieter Claesz Soutman. His prints copied painters from Haarlem such as Nicolaes Berchem, Adriaen van Ostade, Pieter van Laer and Adriaen Brouwer. He also made a series of portraits of religious figures from Amsterdam and Haarlem. In 1653 he joined the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke. His work influenced Dirk Helmbreker and Cornelis Bega.

Cort lived his last twelve years in Italy, where people called him Cornelio Fiammingo. He came from Hoorn or Edam, and his first known engravings came out in Antwerp around 1553, published by Hieronymus Cock. In 1565 he moved to Venice and lived in the house of Titian, and he engraved many of Titian's works. Later he went on to Bologna and Rome, and in Rome he founded a school of engraving. He may also have worked for the Medici in Florence. He is said to have engraved upwards of 151 plates.

Isabey wanted to be a sailor, but his father insisted that he study painting. After lessons with his father and copying at the Louvre, he shared a studio at Honfleur with the landscape painter Xavier Leprince in 1824. In 1831 he turned down a place on a diplomatic mission to Morocco, so his friend Delacroix went instead. Isabey became a court painter to King Louis-Philippe, and he painted the return of Napoleon's remains aboard the Belle Poule. He also painted many storms and shipwrecks. His students included Eugène Boudin and Johan Barthold Jongkind.

Verneuil took his ideas from Japanese art and from nature, especially the sea. He learned his trade from the Swiss designer Eugène Grasset. His bold floral designs went onto ceramic tiles, wallpapers and furnishing textiles, and he also made posters in France alongside artists such as Toulouse-Lautrec and Chéret. After the First World War he moved to Geneva. In 1923 he set off with his wife Adélaïde Verneuil de Marval, who was also a painter, on a long voyage to the Far East. He trained many artists, among them Amédée Ozenfant.

Mortimer's father was a customs officer who also dealt in flour and owned several mills. By 1757 the son was studying in London at the Duke of Richmond's Academy, where he became friends with Joseph Wright. In 1759 he won a first prize for a study after Michelangelo's Bacchus. The Society of Artists gave him prizes for paintings of British history, and he became its president in 1774. He painted the figures for several of Thomas Jones's landscapes. He died at 39.

Modersohn-Becker painted many self-portraits, some of them nudes. She grew up in Dresden as the third of seven children, and her father worked as an engineer for the German railway. In 1888 the family moved to Bremen. She is recognised as the first known woman painter to paint nude self-portraits, and she is believed to be the first woman artist to show herself pregnant. A museum devoted only to her work opened in 1927. She died at 31.
